triage.name: Color Blindness
triage.reason: Hereditary vision defect detected by history and simple testing; reasonable pediatric or primary care case though limited workup.

auto-repaired: workup: 'optical coherence tomography of the macula and optic nerve' was in ['supporting', 'not_indicated'], kept ['not_indicated', 'supporting']

demographics: Red-green color vision defects are X-linked recessive and affect roughly 1 in 12 males of Northern European descent versus about 1 in 200 females
Blue-yellow defects affect males and females about equally
Often first noticed during school screening or when a child is learning colors

risk_factors.text: Family history of color vision deficiency, especially in maternal male relatives
Occupational or hobby exposure to solvents, lead or other neurotoxins

family_history: Color vision deficiency in a brother, maternal uncle or maternal grandfather

chief_complaints.text: I have trouble telling some colors apart
I can't pass the color test at school
Reds and greens look the same to me

hpi.onset: Present since birth or early childhood; often noticed when the patient is learning colors or takes a vision screening test
hpi.progression: Non-progressive; the patient has always seen colors this way and has learned to compensate
hpi.location: Both eyes, affecting color perception rather than sharpness
hpi.quality: Specific colors are confused or look washed out; brightness and clarity of vision are otherwise normal
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually does not limit daily activities, though it can affect school tasks and career choices
aggravating: Small or similarly shaded color-coded items such as maps, wires or traffic signals
relieving: Using labels, patterns or position cues instead of color

associated_symptoms.text: Difficulty matching or naming colors as a child
Trouble reading color-coded charts, maps or graphs
Difficulty distinguishing ripe fruit or meat doneness
Mildly reduced ability to see faint color differences in dim light

pertinent_negatives: Pain or redness in the eye
Family history of progressive vision loss

argues_against: Sudden onset of color vision loss
Associated vision loss or eye pain
Focal neurologic deficits suggesting optic neuritis or stroke

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not report a problem at all; it is usually found on school vision screening or when a parent notices difficulty naming colors.
Acquired color vision loss is more likely than a hereditary defect and is often due to cataracts, macular degeneration, optic nerve disease or medications; it may be asymmetric or progressive.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; normal growth and development
general.moderate: Well-appearing, comfortable; may hesitate or make errors when asked to name colors
general.severe: Well-appearing, comfortable; complete inability to identify certain colors but no systemic illness
general.critical: Not applicable; hereditary color vision deficiency is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Show Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates under good lighting and ask the patient to identify the number or shape in each plate
findings.finding: Errors on multiple plates, especially red-green plates; the pattern of errors helps classify the defect

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to name or match colored objects (e.g., red and green pens, color-coded charts)
findings.finding: Confusion or misnaming of red and green (or blue and yellow) shades

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity with a Snellen chart in each eye
findings.finding: Normal or near-normal visual acuity, typically 20/20 to 20/30

findings.maneuver: Confrontation visual field testing in each eye
Test pupillary light reflex and swinging flashlight test
findings.finding: Equal, reactive pupils without afferent pupillary defect
Normal optic discs, macula, vessels and retina
Full, conjugate eye movements without nystagmus or strabismus

findings.maneuver: Perform color vision testing in a patient with suspected acquired color loss (e.g., optic neuritis, medication toxicity)
findings.finding: Normal color vision, arguing against an acquired cause

initial.why: Standard screening test for red-green color vision deficiency; errors on multiple plates confirm the defect and the pattern helps classify it
Orders and classifies the color confusion when Ishihara is abnormal or a blue-yellow defect is suspected
Confirms that sharpness of vision is normal, separating an isolated color defect from other eye disease
Looks for a scotoma or field loss that would point to optic nerve or retinal disease

initial.test: Pupillary light reflex and swinging flashlight test
initial.why: An afferent pupillary defect suggests optic nerve disease rather than a hereditary color defect
Normal discs and macula support a hereditary cone defect and argue against acquired causes

confirmatory.why: Detailed arrangement test that quantifies and classifies the axis of color loss when the diagnosis is uncertain
Most precise test; distinguishes protan from deutan defects and confirms the diagnosis when screening tests are equivocal

supporting.why: An X-linked pattern with affected maternal male relatives supports a hereditary red-green defect

supporting.test: Optical coherence tomography of the macula and optic nerve
supporting.why: Only if fundoscopy is abnormal or an acquired cause is suspected
supporting.only_if: fundoscopic examination is abnormal or an acquired cause is suspected

not_indicated.why: No role in an isolated, lifelong color vision defect
No role in an isolated, lifelong color vision defect
Not part of the evaluation of hereditary color vision deficiency
Not part of the evaluation of hereditary color vision deficiency

not_indicated.test: MRI brain and orbits with contrast
not_indicated.why: Reserved for suspected optic neuritis, mass lesion or other acquired optic nerve disease, not for a stable hereditary defect

not_indicated.test: Optical coherence tomography of the macula and optic nerve
not_indicated.why: Not routine; only when fundoscopy is abnormal or an acquired cause is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: fundoscopic examination is abnormal or an acquired cause is suspected

decision_points: A stable, lifelong, bilateral color confusion with normal acuity, fields, pupils and fundus is hereditary and needs no further workup
Sudden or progressive color loss, asymmetric findings, or an afferent pupillary defect should prompt evaluation for optic neuritis, medication toxicity or retinal disease
Review medications such as hydroxychloroquine, ethambutol, digoxin and sildenafil when color vision changes are new

differential.name: Optic neuritis
differential.why_considered: Acquired color vision loss, especially red desaturation, can be mistaken for a color vision defect
differential.trigger: Sudden or subacute color vision loss, often unilateral, with pain on eye movement

history: Sudden onset over hours to days
May have prior neurologic symptoms or a demyelinating history
exam: Afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye
Central scotoma on visual field testing
labs: May have abnormal inflammatory or autoimmune markers if an underlying systemic disease is present
imaging: Optic nerve enhancement on MRI of the orbits
White matter lesions on brain MRI in demyelinating disease

differential.name: Cataracts
differential.why_considered: Lens opacity can cause gradual color vision changes, especially blue-yellow confusion and dimming of colors

history: Older age or prior eye trauma or steroid use
exam: Reduced visual acuity that improves with refraction
Normal color vision testing when acuity is corrected

differential.name: Macular degeneration
differential.why_considered: Macular disease can cause acquired color vision changes and central visual distortion

history: Gradual onset, often in older adults
exam: Drusen, pigmentary changes or hemorrhage on fundoscopy
imaging: Macular changes on optical coherence tomography
Drusen or atrophy on fundus examination

differential.name: Diabetic retinopathy
differential.why_considered: Retinal vascular disease can cause acquired color vision loss and visual symptoms

history: Floaters or sudden visual loss if hemorrhage occurs
exam: Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates or neovascularization on fundoscopy
Color vision changes that are typically asymmetric or progressive
imaging: Fluorescein angiography showing leakage or ischemia
Optical coherence tomography showing macular edema

differential.name: Amblyopia
differential.why_considered: Reduced vision in one eye from abnormal visual development can be associated with color vision testing difficulty

history: Reduced vision in one eye since childhood
History of strabismus, anisometropia or visual deprivation
exam: Reduced visual acuity in one eye not correctable with refraction
Normal color vision when tested monocularly in the better eye
imaging: Normal optic nerve and macula on fundoscopy

differential.name: Retinitis pigmentosa
differential.why_considered: Inherited retinal degeneration can cause progressive color vision loss, especially blue-yellow, along with night blindness

imaging: Electroretinogram showing reduced rod and cone responses
Optical coherence tomography showing retinal thinning

severity.mild: Mild red-green deficiency: confuses only similar shades; passes most daily tasks; may be unaware until tested
severity.moderate: Moderate red-green deficiency: clear confusion between red and green; difficulty with color-coded charts, maps or signals; may affect school or occupational tasks
severity.severe: Severe or complete color vision deficiency: cannot distinguish red from green or blue from yellow; may have markedly reduced color discrimination; rare complete achromatopsia with photophobia and nystagmus
severity.critical: Not applicable; hereditary color vision deficiency is not a life-threatening condition

red_flags.finding: Sudden or rapidly progressive color vision loss
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an acquired cause such as optic neuritis, stroke, or medication toxicity, not a hereditary defect

red_flags.finding: Unilateral color vision loss or asymmetric findings
red_flags.meaning: Points to acquired optic nerve or retinal disease
Indicates optic nerve dysfunction and requires urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Associated vision loss, eye pain, or visual field defect
red_flags.meaning: Suggests acquired ocular or neurologic disease rather than an isolated hereditary color defect

red_flags.finding: New color vision changes in a patient taking hydroxychloroquine, ethambutol, digoxin, or sildenafil
red_flags.meaning: Possible medication toxicity; requires prompt review and possible discontinuation

complications.name: Occupational and safety limitations
clues: Difficulty with color-coded wiring, traffic signals, or aviation or maritime signaling

complications.name: School and learning difficulties
clues: Trouble with color-coded maps, charts, or graphs

complications.name: Psychological or social impact
clues: Embarrassment or frustration when naming colors

special_populations.differences: Often detected on school vision screening or when learning colors; may not report symptoms; testing should use age-appropriate methods such as Ishihara plates for older children or simplified color matching for younger children.

Acquired color vision loss from cataracts, macular degeneration, optic nerve disease, or medications is more likely than a hereditary defect; onset is often progressive or asymmetric and warrants evaluation for underlying disease.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice trouble with colors — has it been this way as long as you can remember, or did it change recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Lifelong, stable pattern suggests hereditary defect; new or progressive change suggests acquired disease

key_questions.question: Which colors do you mix up, and in what situations?
key_questions.looking_for: Red and green confusion (most common) versus blue and yellow confusion

key_questions.question: Is it the same in both eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Symmetric bilateral involvement supports hereditary defect; asymmetric or unilateral suggests optic nerve or retinal disease

key_questions.question: Has your sharpness of vision changed, or do you have blurring, distortion, or trouble reading?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in isolated color vision deficiency; present suggests another eye disease

key_questions.question: Any eye pain, redness, tearing, light sensitivity, floaters, or flashes?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present points to acquired ocular or neurologic disease

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family — especially your mother's brothers or your mother's father — have trouble telling colors apart?
key_questions.looking_for: X-linked pattern with affected maternal male relatives supports hereditary red-green defect

key_questions.question: Did you have trouble learning colors as a child, or fail a color vision test at school?
key_questions.looking_for: Childhood onset and school screening failure support a congenital defect

key_questions.question: Do you take any medications, especially hydroxychloroquine, ethambutol, digoxin, or sildenafil?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that can cause acquired color vision loss or toxicity

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a head injury, stroke, seizure, or diagnosis like multiple sclerosis?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic history that would suggest an acquired cause such as optic neuritis

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, or any other chronic illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions associated with retinopathy or optic nerve disease

key_questions.question: Does your work or a hobby expose you to solvents, lead, or other chemicals?
key_questions.looking_for: Toxin exposure that can cause acquired color vision loss

key_questions.question: Has the color problem ever come on suddenly or gotten worse over days to weeks?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden or rapid progression suggests an acquired, potentially urgent cause rather than a hereditary defect

reasoning_points: Lifelong, stable, bilateral color confusion with no change over time
Specific confusion between red and green shades (or blue and yellow)
Normal visual acuity, visual fields, pupils, and fundoscopic examination
Errors on multiple Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates
Family history consistent with X-linked recessive inheritance, especially affected maternal male relatives
No red flags such as sudden onset, unilateral involvement, afferent pupillary defect, eye pain, or new medication exposure

easy: Young boy who fails a school color vision screening
Classic red-green confusion on Ishihara plates
Family history of color blindness in maternal male relatives
medium: Adult who was never tested but has lifelong difficulty with color-coded charts or wiring
Blue-yellow defect rather than the more common red-green pattern
Patient taking a medication that can affect color vision, requiring the student to distinguish hereditary from acquired
Mild defect with only a few errors on testing
hard: Older adult with new or progressive color vision changes from cataracts, macular degeneration, or optic nerve disease
Unilateral or asymmetric color loss suggesting optic neuritis
Patient on hydroxychloroquine or ethambutol with subtle color changes
Young child too young for standard Ishihara testing, requiring simplified color matching
Coexisting amblyopia or other visual problem that complicates interpretation
